chapter: Learning from Fletcher's circle in New York
title: What was taught at Hawkins' sessions: chords for Harrison, Red Allen, Bailey
summary: Hawkins explained chord notes to Jimmy Harrison and told Henry Red Allen his diminished-chord runs were wrong but sounded good. Horace then praises Don Redman as arranger and rehearser and mentions Charlie Dixon.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: When you were having these talk sessions -- jam sessions and so on at Hawkins' house -- apartment, what sorts of things were talked about? I mean, like you say, you play through something, and then they would say, 'Okay, we did this, we did that.' Do you recall some of the things that were really said?

Yes. Yes. I'll tell you why. Coleman Hawkins was a thorough musician, chordwise, you know. He'd played the melody in his own accompaniment in order to do that, so to speak, like they played 'Body and Soul,' remember and go around and dip down how he used to play the melody (inaudible) and play these chords. A lot of the fellas respected him in Fletcher's band. So much so that they would like to know what notes were in that particular thing, and Hawk would -- on his chorus -- would we would be jamming something, and Jimmy Harrison had a great

ear. Jimmy Harrison was a great trombonist. He knew nothing about chords or anything. He just played the way he felt in his heart, but he wanted to learn how -- what notes were in certain chords, and Hawk would tell him, you know. And other guys would ask -- the trumpet player -- Henry Red Allen, incidentally, was in on this session too. And he was one of the few trumpet players that I know of that could run a diminished chord against a major and make it sound good. He'd invert it on the end and come back to the chord. But he didn't know what he was doin'. But it sound good. Like you would play like a E flat chord, like (Sings Chord). Red would play (Sings Chord), and turn it in, you know. So Hawk said -- would tell him, "That's wrong, but it sounds good, keep it in." He'd say, "Well, what am I doing?" We'd ask those things, you know. Guys would ask those things. And I didn't write that down, you know. It was a session that was actually to help everybody, and they got so that they would -- wouldn't -- would try things out and take another tune, and use these particular little points that Hawk would tell 'em. Buster Bailey was another one. He was so fast on his clarinet that he could -- he was just an executionist, we'll say. And of course, this didn't bother him much, so Hawk didn't interfere with that.
Don Redmon, who was one of the greatest arrangers, in my estimation, and one of the greatest rehearsers of a band --

he was Fletcher's first alto saxophonist and arranger, one of the very first ones with Fletcher. Even before Fletcher had started to really get out into the arranging field, Don first started Fletcher's book -- Don Redmond. And of course the guitarist, Charlie Dixon, from over in New Jersey was another guy that picked up arranging and turned out to be terrific.
